newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Better security may release Congo robusta coffee.
newsitem.headline: Better security may release Congo robusta coffee.

text.p: Robusta coffee trapped by fighting in the interior of the Democratic Republic of Congo will be exported over the next month if security does not worsen, dealers say.

Dealers' estimates for the amount so far held up after the takeover by President Laurent Kabila's forces range between 6,000 and 9,000 tonnes -- increasing as the region heads into the main buying season.
"Two boats have already gone up there to buy, and there are boats there already loaded and waiting to come down," said one Kinshasa-based buyer.
"Because the prices have been good this year our people up there are demanding ever more money and saying there is lots to buy from the farmers," said another dealer in the Congo capital.

The advance of Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL) cut the capital off from the main robusta region in the tropical basin, which covers the north and centre of the vast state.
Most buying in Kinshasa stopped around the end of April, near the beginning of the season for the equatorial region, which tails off towards November.
The AFDL reached the capital on May 17, when Kabila proclaimed himself president, but dealers say that security is far from complete in some robusta-growing pockets.
Parts of the region lie in the heartland of ousted president Mobutu Sese Seko, and dealers say that not only have Kabila's troops not penetrated to all parts, but that it is not seen as a priority.

"There is still looting going on up there, maybe there are Mobutu loyalists, maybe Alliance troops, we don't know, but some parts of the country are still no-go areas," said one Kinshasa- based buyer and plantation owner.
Transport is via the network of rivers which feather out from the Congo river, leading to Kinshasa and its link to the Atlantic port of Matadi.
Total production of robustas in 1996 was over 43,000 tonnes according to the central bank, against almost 47,000 tonnes in 1995 and 55,000 tonnes in 1994.
In the long term Congolese dealers see growth in exports linked to improvements in political stability, transport infrastructure and financing.
But the primary factor is world prices which very quickly feed through to farmers.

"Higher prices this year are likely to mean some increase because there will be greater efforts to get the crop to market, but any major increase would have to wait until next season if strong prices are sustained," said one buyer.

Dealers said that when London benchmark robusta futures stood at around $2,100 per tonne, the Kinshasa price for medium grade coffee, with very low moisture content, was between $1.20 and $1.30 per kilo.
The eastern reaches of the robusta growing region in Upper Congo have been badly hit by the tracheomycosis fungus, but the disease has yet to spread to the heart of the central basin.
Traditionally, Congo's main export market for robustas is among instant coffee roasters in Italy, where coffee is drunk sweet and strength is a more important quality than flavour.
